name: Freya Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for agreeing to talk, Freya. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not connected to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and nothing you tell me will have your name on it. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the paper mill, which is basically the reason our town exists. I'm on the rewinder, the machine that takes the giant reels off the paper machine and cuts them down into smaller rolls for customers. I thread the paper, set the knives to the widths on the order sheet, watch for breaks, and label and wrap the finished rolls. I've been there two years and I'm still not as quick at threading as the others.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's good about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's steady. Same shift pattern, same people, I know where I stand. The worst is a paper break at speed, when the whole web tears and you've got to rethread with everyone waiting on you. My partner Tom drives a delivery lorry, so he's out early and I'm on lates some weeks. We do darts at the club on Thursdays, that's our night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I never trusted it anyway. People at work talk about it like it's going to arrive next Tuesday. I'm not online much, but I'd say it at the club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that's the best news I could get. I don't like change, never have. I just want to get good at my job and keep it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing. Keep doing my shifts, keep putting a bit by. We've got about four months of money saved, and I'd keep building that slowly for a deposit on a house one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like when you've been told a test result is fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools yourself at the moment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't use it. I've got a phone for messages and the bank. Tom uses the map on his. Some of the younger ones at work ask the chatbot things, but I'd rather ask Ken, the shift lead. He's been there thirty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If it automated some routine tasks at the mill, which ones would you expect?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The order system, maybe. It's on a computer already. If it got a bit cleverer, fine. As long as it doesn't touch the rewinder.

S0.say: Good, I never trusted it anyway; people talk like it's arriving next Tuesday. I'm not online much, but I'd say it at the club.
S0.think: That's the best news I could get, because I don't like change. I just want to get good at my job and keep it.
S0.do: Carries on with her shifts and keeps saving slowly from about four months of money towards a house deposit. Keeps asking the shift lead rather than using AI tools. Accepts small changes to the order system.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved, like getting a good test result.
S0.quote: People at work talk about it like it's going to arrive next Tuesday.
S0.fieldNote: Freya is plain about not liking change, and she doesn't dress it up. She trusts people with experience, like Ken, over tools. The mill is the town's main employer, which matters for every other scenario.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a business, they'll do what makes sense for them. That's how it's always been. I wouldn't make a fuss about it publicly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be worried. I'm the slowest threader on the shift and the newest. If they get a rewinder that threads itself, and I've heard they exist, I'm the first one they don't need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder and stop eating out, try to get from four months to six. I'd keep my head down and make sure I'm never late, never off sick. And I'd wait and see what they actually announce, because rumours fly round the mill all the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Knotted up. I don't sleep well when things are uncertain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about learning something new, like a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not a course, no. I'm not a classroom person. If they showed me on the machine, I'd learn. Ken taught me everything that way. Put me in front of a screen with a video and I glaze over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you did lose your place on the rewinder, where would you go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somewhere else local. There's the packaging plant and the frozen food factory on the bypass. I'd rather do the same sort of work somewhere else than start something I'm bad at.

S1.say: It's a business and they'll do what makes sense for them, like always. I wouldn't make a fuss publicly.
S1.think: I'm the slowest threader on the shift and the newest. If they get a rewinder that threads itself, I'm the first one they don't need.
S1.do: Saves harder and stops eating out, aiming to go from four to six months. Keeps her head down with perfect attendance and waits for real announcements. Looks at the packaging plant or frozen food factory on the bypass if she's let go.
S1.feel: Knotted up and sleeping badly with the uncertainty.
S1.quote: Put me in front of a screen with a video and I glaze over.
S1.fieldNote: Her public 'it's a business' line hides real fear about being the slowest and newest. She'd learn hands-on from a person but rejects classroom or video training. Her escape route is the same kind of work elsewhere, which she knows exists locally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't believe it, at first. Then probably that someone should have stopped it. I'm not political, but that's a lot of people at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully? Tom's lorry and my rewinder, both gone in two years. We've got four months saved. In a town where the mill is everything, there's nowhere to go. I don't know what I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut right back the same week, cancel anything we pay for monthly, stop the car insurance on my old car and sell it. I'd talk to my mum and dad about moving in with them, they're forty minutes away in a bigger town. And I'd sign up for whatever help the government put out, even though I'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Terrified. I think I'd just sit in the car after the shift and not want to go in the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can't do anything about it in two years. Other people can study or move. I'd still be trying to understand what the thing even is when it's taken my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hold on to, if you were cutting everything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Darts, probably. Sounds daft. But it's the one night we don't think about anything. We'd keep that if it was the last thing we paid for.

S2.say: I wouldn't believe it at first, then I'd say someone should have stopped it. I'm not political, but that's a lot of people at once.
S2.think: Tom's lorry and my rewinder both go in two years and we've only got four months saved. In a town where the mill is everything, there's nowhere to go.
S2.do: Cuts every monthly cost the same week and sells her old car. Asks her parents about moving in with them in a bigger town forty minutes away. Signs up for government help despite hating it.
S2.feel: Terrified, with an image of sitting in the car after a shift not wanting to go inside.
S2.quote: I'd still be trying to understand what the thing even is when it's taken my job.
S2.fieldNote: The double hit on two incomes in a one-employer town leaves her with no options she believes in. She moves from 'not political' to 'someone should have stopped it' in one breath. Keeping Thursday darts was a small, telling act of holding on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'd better start getting ready, then. Five years isn't long. I'd say it to Tom and my mum, not to the internet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still be thirty-two with nothing else I'm good at. Five years helps with money, but I don't think I'd become a different person in five years. I'm not built for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save every month, really push it, aim for a year of money by the time it comes. Tom and I were going to get married next summer, and I think we'd put that off and keep the money. I'd stay at the mill as long as it lasted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but I'd have something to do with it, like a long countdown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're putting off the wedding. Isn't that giving up a lot for a 'maybe'?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't want to be. But you lose the house you haven't bought yet and the wedding you haven't had. That's a lot to give up for something that might not happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Tom do in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom would want to go to his cousin's, who drives for a big firm, see if there's work. He's braver than me. I'd go along, I suppose. Somebody has to keep the savings safe.

S3.say: We'd better start getting ready, because five years isn't long. I'd say it to Tom and my mum, not to the internet.
S3.think: I'd be thirty-two with nothing else I'm good at. Five years helps with money, but I'm not built to become a different person.
S3.do: Saves hard every month aiming for a year of money by 2031. Postpones next summer's wedding with Tom to keep the money. Stays at the mill as long as it lasts.
S3.feel: Scared, but with something to do, like a long countdown.
S3.quote: You lose the house you haven't bought yet and the wedding you haven't had.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives her money time but not, in her view, time to change. Postponing the wedding is a real cost she weighs out loud. She sees herself as the cautious one guarding the savings while Tom looks for openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long way off and most things they predict don't happen on time. I'd probably say that a lot. It's what my dad says about everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it would still be at the back of my mind. But ten years means I could actually get good at my job and save up. Maybe they'd keep a few people on to watch the machines, and I'd want to be one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at the mill, save a bit more each year, and get married next summer like we planned. I'd wait and see for the first few years. If it looked real by halfway, then I'd think about what next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Some nights I'd think about it, most nights I wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Waiting until halfway, is that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. That's how I am. Tom says I'd wait for the flood to reach the doorstep before moving the sofa. But I'd have savings by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the mill would come out of this one best?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ken. Ten years from now he'd want to retire anyway. He'd be the lucky one, going out on his own terms.

S4.say: Ten years is a long way off and most predictions don't happen on time. It's what my dad says about everything.
S4.think: It would sit at the back of my mind, but ten years means I could get good at my job and save. Maybe they'd keep a few people on to watch the machines, and I'd want to be one.
S4.do: Stays at the mill, saves a bit more each year and goes ahead with the wedding next summer. Waits and sees for the first few years before deciding anything. Plans to rethink only if it looks real by the halfway point.
S4.feel: Uneasy, thinking about it some nights but not most.
S4.quote: Tom says I'd wait for the flood to reach the doorstep before moving the sofa.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade she falls back on her family's scepticism about predictions and keeps her plans. She knows waiting is her weakness and repeats Tom's joke about it herself. Hoping to be one of the few kept on to watch the machines was her only forward-looking idea.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time and both of us lose our jobs in a town with one big employer. What would help is someone keeping the mill going with people in it for longer, even if it's less efficient. And proper training on the machine, by a person, not on a laptop.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: How it feels to be the slow one. Everyone talks about people who'll do well. Nobody asks the ones who were already behind before any of this started.

headlineQuote: Nobody asks the ones who were already behind before any of this started.
portrait: Freya is 27 and two years into running the rewinder at the paper mill that her small town depends on, living with her partner Tom, a lorry driver, and saving slowly from about four months of money. She dislikes change, never uses AI tools and learns best hands-on from veterans like Ken. She'd be calm in a plateau, anxious but quiet under steady change, and panicked by fast AGI because it takes both incomes in a one-employer town. More warning time mostly gives her time to save and delay, not to become someone new.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time and both she and Tom would lose their jobs in a town with one big employer.
whatWouldHelp: Keeping the mill running with people in it for longer, even if it's less efficient, and hands-on training from a person rather than a laptop.
